structure.title: Chapters I–II · What is the proposed standard?
structure.text: Mill begins with disagreement over morals, then defends happiness as the end by which action should be assessed. The distinction between pleasures of different quality answers an opponent who thinks this standard gives people too little to live for.

structure.title: Chapters III–IV · Why follow it, and what supports it?
structure.text: The feeling of obligation and the evidence for an ultimate end receive separate examinations. The fact that someone desires a good and the claim that everyone ought to count each person's good both figure in the argument, but they are distinct steps.

structure.title: Chapter V · The protest made in the name of justice
structure.text: Rights, punishment, desert and fairness seem to exert a force that ordinary calculations of convenience lack. Mill takes that experience seriously enough to ask what protects a person's security and why its violation arouses such fierce resentment.

people.name: The competent judge
people.role: A witness acquainted with both pleasures
people.text: Mill gives weight to the preference of someone who knows both sides of a comparison. The argument makes experience indispensable and raises a further question about who gets admitted as a qualified witness.

people.name: Security
people.text: A person expecting violence or confiscation tomorrow cannot freely pursue most of the goods available today. Mill uses this dependence to explain why justice can feel different in kind from a modest gain in convenience.

context.title: Happiness has more than one owner
context.text: A person's own pleasure has a place in the reckoning alongside everyone else's. Several familiar objections become clearer once a question about personal motive is separated from the proposed standard for judging an act.

notice.text: Follow money and virtue as desires change.
notice.why: Something first pursued for what it buys may become desired in its own right. Mill uses this familiar change to explain how ends can multiply inside a theory organised around happiness.

notice.text: Compare disputes where both sides appeal to justice.
notice.why: Equal pay and pay according to contribution can each sound indisputably fair. Once the slogans collide, Mill asks what could decide between them.

opening: If an action makes people's lives better, that seems a powerful reason to do it. Trouble begins when one person's happiness comes at another's expense, or when a satisfying life requires more than accumulating pleasures. Mill takes the apparently simple idea that morality should serve happiness and works through its most troublesome implications. Justice, sacrifice, and the quality of enjoyment become tests of whether a principle meant to take everyone's welfare seriously can explain the obligations people are least willing to trade away.
